title.value: A Place Further Than the Universe

logline: Four high school girls embark on an Antarctic expedition together - one driven by grief over a missing mother, the others by restlessness, loneliness, and a hunger for something that actually matters.

renewal.note: The 13-episode original anime by Madhouse aired from January to March 2018 and concluded as a complete standalone story. No sequel has been produced or announced.

bollymeter.basis: MAL score of 8.50 from a large voting base; Anime News Network episode reviewers consistently praised the series for its emotional architecture, with ANN user weighted mean at 8.40 (Very Good+) and 86 votes of Masterpiece.

pull_quotes.text: It's been able to achieve its modest narrative ambitions without any trouble, and that foundation should give it plenty to build on.

seasons.review_body: Madhouse's original 2018 anime - broadcast on AT-X and Tokyo MX - is widely considered one of the finest anime of that decade. Directed by Atsuko Ishizuka and written by Jukki Hanada, the series uses the Antarctic expedition as both a literal and emotional destination. The four leads are distinct and credibly teenage; their reasons for attempting something this extreme are grounded in recognisable adolescent longing rather than fantasy. Anime News Network's episodic reviewers tracked the series' slow emotional build across 13 weeks, consistently noting how the show layers meaning into its visual design and character dynamics before delivering its most emotionally powerful episodes. The finale is among the most discussed in recent anime history. The series earned simulcast status on Crunchyroll and won the Anime of the Year award at the Crunchyroll Anime Awards in 2019.

episode_reviews.title: One Million Yen Worth of Youth
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Mari Tamaki has lived a life of almost-adventures and abandoned dreams. When she meets Shirase Kobuchizawa, who has spent years saving a million yen to reach Antarctica, the premise snaps into focus immediately. The premiere is warm, propulsive, and confidently specific.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A million yen spilling from a bag - the most concrete expression of years of single-minded resolve any anime premiere has offered.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# A Place Further Than The Universe S1E1: "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Kimari** opens on a nightmare so ridiculous it loops back into truth: her mother trying to kill her with a wet towel. The detail is silly. The fear underneath is clean. Home, school, routine, the same day repeating until youth becomes something she remembers planning instead of living. So she chooses Tokyo, a place far enough to count. BollyAI's read: this premiere works because it understands that a big journey often begins as a badly organised escape.

## The Wet Towel Sets the Trap

The first smart move in "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" is that **Kimari** begins as a girl frightened by a dream, then by the shape of her own normal life. The wet towel nightmare gives the episode a comic jolt while naming her problem. Safety has started to feel like suffocation.

That is why the Tokyo plan matters. At school, she decides she has to take action during high school and lands on an aimless journey. The word "aimless" matters. The episode is selling movement as proof that Kimari can still surprise herself. She prepares to run away alone and rides away from school life, but the plan already wobbles. She wants rebellion more than she has built rebellion.

The pacing helps. The early quiet stretches let Kimari's dissatisfaction sit before the plot starts moving faster. The episode saves Antarctica for later and first makes the smaller dream feel hard. Skipping school, leaving alone, changing a story on a phone call. These are modest actions, but for Kimari they are the first test of whether she can turn wanting into doing.

The weakness is visible too. The premiere has a lot of machinery to set, and parts of the middle lean on explanation rather than discovery. Still, the opening has a clean emotional engine: Kimari is less bored than afraid that she will never become the person who leaves.

## Tokyo Is the Decoy

The Tokyo trip is the hour's clever fake destination. Kimari chooses it because it is reachable, vague, and just irresponsible enough to feel like youth. The episode frames it as an "aimless journey," then quietly exposes the limit of that fantasy. A trip without purpose can break routine, but it cannot fill the space underneath.

That is where the title's idea of worth starts to bite. One million yen enters the story as the object that starts a search, and the question of who dropped it becomes one of the premiere's open loops. The money functions as more than a prop. It pulls Kimari out of private hesitation and into someone else's impossible plan. Cash, here, is effort made physical. It can be lost. It can be chased. It can become evidence that a dream has been worked for, not merely spoken aloud.

Kimari's contradiction gives the episode its best small character turn. She wants to run away alone, but when the moment comes, she does not vanish into her own teenage movie. She helps by calling the school and changing her story. That choice shifts her from escape to participation. She is still moving away from routine, now with another person attached to the movement.

BollyAI's read: the premiere understands the difference between wanderlust and direction. Kimari thinks she needs distance. The story hands her a purpose and watches her recognise the upgrade.

## Antarctica Enters Like a Dare

Then **Kobuchizawa Shirase** arrives with a dream so concrete that it makes Kimari's Tokyo plan look like a practice swing. Her mother wrote about Antarctica, went missing, and was never found. Shirase does not soften the sentence into romance. She makes it a mission: "So, I'm going to find her."

That line turns the episode. Until then, the hour has followed a girl desperate to do something before youth hardens into memory. After it, the question sharpens. What happens when the something is absurd, expensive, public, and tied to grief? Shirase wants to go to Antarctica to find her mother, and the premiere gives that goal a practical spine through the one million yen and her insistence that she has been working. The dream is huge, but the proof is mundane. Work. Money. Repetition. Refusal.

The skepticism around her goal matters. The question "To Antarctica? Is it possible?" captures the wall the premiere keeps putting in front of Shirase. Her dream sounds impossible because people keep treating it that way. That resistance sharpens her. She is not asking for approval. She is trying to force belief through action.

The middle stretch gets dense as Shirase's backstory and intent arrive. That density makes the emotional math clear, though it presses down on the mystery too firmly. The missing mother, the cash, the school search, the Antarctica ambition. The episode stacks the pieces fast. The writing survives because Shirase's motive is plain and strong enough to carry the load.

## Rooting Is an Action Here

One of the episode's gentler pivots comes when someone sees Shirase, wants to talk, and says they are rooting for her. In a weaker version, that support would be decorative. Here, it becomes part of the hour's argument. Belief changes what people are willing to do next.

Kimari's support is awkward, partial, and right for a first episode. She does not become fearless in one scene. She does not suddenly match Shirase's intensity. She alters her own plan around someone else's need. The phone call to school, the changed story, the willingness to help. These are modest moves, and the premiere treats that modesty as honest. Teenage courage gets to be messy before it becomes cinematic.

That is why the search through freshmen rooms matters as texture. The episode keeps bringing private desire into shared spaces. A missing girl, a dropped fortune, people asking if the person they are looking for is there. Shirase's Antarctica plan could have remained a solitary obsession. Instead, the mechanics of the plot keep making it visible to others. Once seen, it cannot stay safely impossible.

The title says "One Million Yen Worth of Youth," and the hour earns that phrase by refusing to make youth a mood board. It is money saved, lies improvised, plans half-made, and the first person who says they are rooting for you when everyone else hears Antarctica and thinks of failure.

## The Ship Gives the Dream a Shape

The strongest late beat is the public opening of the icebreaker Shirase at Kure Port. After an episode full of wanting, explaining, doubting, and chasing, the story finally points to a thing with steel and a schedule. The ship announcement gives the dream its first believable edge of the map.

That matters for Kobuchizawa's central contradiction. She wants to go to Antarctica to find her mother, while living with disbelief around her. Her answer is practical. She pushes others to come next Saturday and check the ship. Look at it, the episode says. Stand near the thing. Let the impossible become an object you can visit.

As a closing move, it is clean. The premiere does not need to put its characters on a vessel. It only needs to make the next step real enough that refusing it would feel like retreat. The ship preview converts Shirase's grief from backstory into direction, and it gives Kimari's aimlessness a place to go.

The limitation is that the episode's late acceleration leaves some emotional beats feeling assigned rather than fully breathed. The one million yen open loop is compelling, but it works more as ignition than as a fully shaped mystery in this hour. Even so, the final plan lands because the episode has done its central job: it turns a vague wish to leave into a specific invitation to follow.

## The Verdict

"One Million Yen Worth of Youth" is a strong premiere because it builds adventure from hesitation. Kimari's failed attempt at aimless escape and Shirase's fixed Antarctica mission sharpen each other. One girl wants proof that she can leave. The other has already chosen where she must go and why. The episode's exposition gets crowded, especially once the money, the missing mother, and the ship all need space, but the emotional line stays clear. BollyAI's read: the hour earns its optimism by making action look difficult before it looks inspiring. As a season opener, it plants two sturdy engines for what follows: whether Antarctica can be reached, and how a dropped one million yen binds Kimari to Shirase's impossible plan.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp premiere that turns teenage restlessness into direction, with Antarctica arriving as grief, dare, and destination.

episode_reviews.title: A Place Further Than the Universe
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers the emotional payoff the series has been building across 12 episodes. The Antarctic setting, the search for what was lost, and the bonds formed during the journey all converge in a sequence that critics and audiences consistently identify as one of the most affecting in contemporary anime.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The email inbox - a scene described by the ANN reviewer as finally delivering the dramatic bite the series had been building toward.

critic_note.text: This episode finally gave me what I wanted most out of this show: a storyline with some genuine dramatic bite.
